name: Asafoetida (Ferula asafoetida resin)
short: Infants: life-threatening methaemoglobinaemia after an asafoetida remedy (case report; authors say avoid in infants). Capsule trials (43, 74 people): no adverse events or no difference.
text: This entry covers asafoetida, the oleo-gum resin of Ferula asafoetida, taken by mouth. Infants: a case report describes life-threatening methaemoglobinaemia (a blood disorder that reduces oxygen delivery), with cyanosis and severe breathing difficulty, in an infant given an asafoetida herbal remedy; the infant's two brothers had glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency, and the infant was treated successfully with high-concentration oxygen. The authors say infants are more susceptible to this disorder and that asafoetida should be avoided as a herbal remedy in infants. An older record with no abstract is titled 'Methemoglobinemia in an infant treated with the folk remedy glycerited asafoetida'. Other trials: in a double-blind, placebo-controlled study, 43 people with functional dyspepsia took capsules of a food-grade asafoetida formulation or placebo for 30 days, and no adverse events or changes in blood tests were reported. In a 1-month study of 74 people with stable severe asthma given oral asafoetida capsules (an oleo-gum resin the abstract calls Ferula foetida) or placebo, the incidence of complications did not differ significantly between groups; the abstract also reports that wheezing improved and that forced vital capacity (a lung-function measure) decreased with asafoetida (the abstract does not discuss the decrease). A 14-day randomized trial in 62 people with dyspepsia symptoms gives no adverse-event figures. Interactions: in healthy volunteers, 4 days of asafoetida changed the urinary breakdown ratios of the test medicine dextromethorphan, raising the CYP2D6 marker ratio by 33% and also raising the CYP3A4 marker ratio; the authors caution about combining asafoetida with medicines broken down by CYP3A4 that have a narrow therapeutic range, such as cyclosporine, tacrolimus and carbamazepine. The cited sources give no data on pregnancy.
